page.layout: Two parallel columns of Latin verse, stanzas in italic: left column first, then right column. Below both columns, two centred lines with the author's name and "POM.". No page number, running head, catchword or signature.

l.i: Noli tuo me protinus Arcere vultu: spiritum Coelestis arrham gratiae Ne prorsus auferas mihi.
Salutis almae gaudium Ah redde fracto: da mihi Alacri ut ultro spiritu, Totum tibi me mancipem.
Non haec tuae indulgentiae Celabo dona ceteros Sontes, sed exemplo meo Ad te redire hos instrua.
Sed me benignus libera, Morte expiando crimine Quansq̃[?] lingua propriam Tuam canet clementiam.
Vero canet: sed abditae Recluda claustra vocule,
Ut cuncta sanctis cantibus Et iubilo circumsonent.
Si victimam me poscere[?], Tibi immolarem victimae: Iusta sed ira percitum, Holocausta te non lenient.
Cor fractum et abiectum malis, Suumque abominans scelus Dolore vero, victima Est gratior quavis tibi.
O sancte rerum conditor Curam Sionis suscipe: Solymae beatae moenia Fulci bonus labantia.
Tum vota soluent debita Tibi pij[?]: tum protinus Aras calentes sanguine Mactatus[?] hircus imbuet.

page.notes: Printer's hook-shaped marks stand before some lines (at "Ah", "Alacri", "Ad", "Ut" and others); they are printer's signs, not text, and were left out. "instrua" at the end of the third stanza may carry a macron over the u; not certain. "Quansq̃" is an abbreviation for quanscunque; the mark is uncertain. "poscere" is followed by a mark that may be a comma or a stop. "pij" may read "piij". "Mactatus" is read from a ct ligature and may be "Maclatus" as printed. The name line may be an attribution rather than a heading; kept as paragraphs.
